title: The Effect of Driving Restrictions on Air Quality in Mexico City
research_question: Did Mexico City's Hoy No Circula program, which prohibits most drivers from using their vehicles one weekday per week based on license plate digits, reduce urban air pollution? How did the policy affect drivers' transportation choices, including the use of public transit, taxis, and private vehicle ownership, and what were the implications for vehicle fleet composition and gasoline consumption?
data_description: The primary data are hourly air pollution measurements from Mexico City's Automated Environmental Monitoring Network for five major pollutants (carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, ozone, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide), along with hourly temperature, humidity, and wind speed, covering 1986–2005, with the main analysis focused on 1986–1993. The unit of observation is an hourly station-level pollution reading, with 5–15 monitoring stations per pollutant. Additional datasets include monthly gasoline sales in Mexico City (1980–2007), monthly subway ridership (1986–2005), monthly public bus ridership (1986–1990), annual counts of registered vehicles and taxis in Mexico City (1980–2005), annual sales of new automobiles (1975–2005), and weekly classified advertisement prices for used taxis and Volkswagen transit vans from El Universal (November 1988–October 1990).
institutional_context: On November 20, 1989, the Mexico City government launched Hoy No Circula in response to record ozone and pollutant levels that routinely exceeded WHO health guidelines. The program prohibits most private and commercial vehicles from circulating one weekday per week, assigned by the last digit of the license plate, between 5:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m. Taxis, buses, emergency vehicles, and certain low-emissions or perishable-goods vehicles were exempt. At launch, restrictions applied to 2.3 million vehicles (about 460,000 per day). Enforcement by city police was vigorous, with violators facing 48-hour impoundment and fines equivalent to roughly US$200, producing near-universal compliance. Mexico City's geography—a high-altitude valley ringed by mountains that trap pollutants—exacerbates air quality problems. The program remains in place and has been emulated in Bogotá, Santiago, and São Paulo, making evaluation of its effects relevant for cities throughout the developing world.
